title: How Carriers Speed Up Policy Comparison: Accurate Review of Unstructured Policy PDFs
summary: How carriers cut policy comparison time on scanned and unstructured policy PDFs, verify every difference against the source clause, and connect results to core systems.
body_markdown:
**Carriers speed up policy comparison by using an insurance-specific AI platform that reads the full policy packet, including scanned pages, base forms, and endorsements, aligns matching sections across documents, and links every difference back to the source clause.** At one mid-sized insurer, FurtherAI ran policy comparisons more than 30 times faster than manual review with equal or better accuracy. Horizontal document-extraction tools can pull text and fields from the same PDFs, but they leave the comparison, the coverage logic, and the audit trail for your team to build.


This guide covers how much time carriers save, why unstructured policy PDFs are hard to compare reliably, how differences get verified, when a horizontal extraction tool is enough, and how comparison results reach your core systems.


## **Key takeaways**


- **Speed comes from reading less by hand, not reading faster.** The platform does the first pass across the full packet, and reviewers confirm flagged differences instead of reading every page.
- **Extraction is only step one.** Comparing policies means aligning sections across documents that use different formats and labels, then working out net coverage across base forms and endorsements.
- **Every difference needs a source.** A redline that links each change to the clause behind it can be confirmed in seconds and defended later.
- **No major cloud extraction service ships a commercial policy model.** Amazon Textract, Azure Document Intelligence, and Google Document AI all require you to set up custom extractors and build the comparison logic yourself.
- **Integration decides the payoff.** Results should write back to the policy administration system instead of living in a separate report.

The time saving comes from changing who does the first read. Instead of an underwriter or analyst reading two 300-page policies side by side, the platform reads both, flags what changed, and hands the reviewer a short list to confirm.


## **What are the best solutions for comparing unstructured policy files?**


The best solutions read the policy the way an experienced reviewer does: every page, every form, and every endorsement, with the relationships between them. That matters because commercial policies rarely arrive as clean data. A typical file mixes native PDFs, scanned endorsements, carrier-specific form layouts, and schedules that run across pages.


Look for four capabilities:


1. **Full-packet reading.**[FurtherAI compares](https://www.furtherai.com/customers/policy-check-compare-ai-teammate) coverage breadth, terms, exclusions, and endorsements, factoring in the full policy packet, including base forms and conditional endorsements.
2. **Section alignment across formats.** Two carriers label the same coverage differently, and the same carrier changes layouts between years. The software has to match equivalent sections before it can compare them.
3. **Net coverage logic.** A base form excludes a peril, an endorsement gives part of it back, and a second endorsement narrows the give-back. FurtherAI identifies these "give-back" endorsements that restore coverage excluded in base policies.
4. **Clause-level redlines.** FurtherAI[redlines limits, deductibles, forms, and endorsements](https://www.furtherai.com/segment/carriers) and lets reviewers jump directly to the changed clauses.


The same insurer also used FurtherAI comparisons to give brokers detailed side-by-side answers to client questions, and to analyze competitor filings from public sources such as SERFF. Brokers comparing quotes across carrier partners can see our guide to[policy comparison software for national brokers](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/policy-comparison-software-national-brokers) .


## **Which tools process complex policy documents most reliably?**


Reliability on complex policies comes down to three things: reading scanned and messy pages correctly, keeping track of where everything sits in a long document, and proving each result against the source.


### Scanned and messy PDFs


Optical character recognition (OCR) is the first point of failure. Scanned endorsements, skewed pages, stamps, and tables that break across pages all degrade the text that downstream models see.[Research on retrieval systems built on OCR output found](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02592) that none of the OCR tools tested was competent for building high-quality knowledge bases, with tables and other complex elements hit hardest.


Length is the second risk. In a[peer-reviewed study of how language models use long inputs](https://aclanthology.org/2024.tacl-1.9/) , performance was often highest when the relevant information sat at the beginning or end of the input, and dropped when it sat in the middle. In a 300-page policy, the clause that matters is often buried deep in the packet.


Insurance-specific platforms handle both by breaking the policy into its parts before comparing.[FurtherAI engineer Frieda Huang built a system](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/inside-building-reliability-into-ai-systems-frieda-huang) that aligns similar sections across multiple policy documents, each more than 300 pages, using semantic similarity to match endorsements and coverage items even when formatting or values differ, with a second layer that groups only items that are directly similar.


### How differences are verified against source clauses


A difference the reviewer can't trace is a difference they have to re-check by hand, which erases the time saving. Verification works in three layers:


- **Citation on every difference.** FurtherAI outputs come with[clickable citations that highlight the areas within your files](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/citations-in-ai) behind each insight, so a reviewer can confirm a change in seconds.
- **Missing items flagged, not filled.** FurtherAI[flags missing information with source citations](https://www.furtherai.com/segment/carriers) instead of guessing.
- **Accuracy measured on your own documents.** With[Eval Studio](https://www.furtherai.com/blog/furtherai-eval-studio) , teams load a test set of real documents, typically 50 or 100, define what a correct result looks like, and score each workflow version before it reaches production.


Auditability also matters for governance. As of October 8, 2026,[29 jurisdictions had adopted the NAIC Model Bulletin on insurers' use of AI](https://content.naic.org/sites/default/files/legal-adoption-map-ai-model-bulletin.pdf) , which expects insurers to maintain governance and documentation for the AI systems they use.


## **Horizontal extraction tools vs insurance-specific platforms**


**For comparing unstructured policies, an insurance-specific platform is the better choice for most carriers.** Horizontal extraction services are a strong foundation for teams with engineering capacity, but they return fields, not comparisons. Insurance-specific platforms start from policy forms, endorsements, and coverage logic, and return differences with citations.


The three largest cloud services are capable extractors:


- [Amazon Textract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/textract/latest/dg/what-is.html) extracts typed and handwritten text, forms, and tables, and processes up to 3,000 pages per asynchronous job.
- [Azure AI Document Intelligence](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/document-intelligence/model-overview) offers read and layout models and processes up to 2,000 pages per PDF.
- [Google Document AI](https://docs.cloud.google.com/document-ai/docs/processors-list) offers OCR, Form Parser, Layout Parser, and a generative Custom Extractor.


None of them ships a prebuilt model for commercial insurance policies or ACORD forms. Azure's only insurance model reads US health insurance cards. Each lets you train custom extractors on labeled samples of your own documents, and the comparison logic, the coverage rules, and the reviewer workflow are yours to build.

## **Frequently asked questions**


#### What software speeds up policy comparison for carriers?


Insurance-specific AI platforms such as FurtherAI speed up policy comparison by reading the full policy packet, aligning matching sections, and redlining differences in limits, deductibles, forms, and endorsements. At one mid-sized insurer, FurtherAI ran comparisons more than 30 times faster than manual review with equal or better accuracy, and a regional carrier reports about 95% faster comparisons.


#### Can AI compare scanned or unstructured policy PDFs accurately?


Yes, when the platform is built for insurance documents and every result links to its source. Scanned pages and long policies are where generic tools struggle most, so look for full-packet reading, section alignment across formats, and a citation on every difference. Test accuracy on 50 to 100 of your own policies before going live.


#### Should carriers compare policies with a horizontal extraction tool or an insurance-specific platform?


For policy comparison, an insurance-specific platform is the better fit for most carriers. Amazon Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, and Google Document AI extract text and fields well, but none ships a prebuilt model for commercial policies, and none aligns sections across two policies or works out net coverage across endorsements. Insurance-specific platforms do both and link each difference to its source clause.


#### How do reviewers verify AI-flagged policy differences?


Each flagged difference should link to the clause it came from. In FurtherAI, citations highlight the exact area of the source file, so a reviewer can confirm or reject a change in seconds. Missing information is flagged rather than filled in, and accuracy can be scored on a test set of your own documents before each workflow change ships.


#### Which platforms integrate with carrier policy administration systems?


FurtherAI reads and writes policy records in Guidewire, Duck Creek, and Majesco through native connectors, runs inside Guidewire PolicyCenter through its accelerator on the Guidewire Marketplace, and reaches legacy systems without APIs through Computer Use 2.0. It can also map data to a carrier's proprietary schema.


#### What does a policy comparison redline include?


A redline lists every difference between two policies, grouped by limits and sublimits, deductibles and retentions, forms and editions, and endorsements and exclusions. A strong one also shows net coverage where an endorsement gives back part of an excluded peril. Each difference should link to the changed clause so a reviewer can confirm it in seconds.
